title: Who truly knows?
hookLine: the oldest Hindu scripture tells how everything began, then asks who really knows
carry: in the vedas, honest questioning is itself sacred

lines: NEITHER WHAT IS NOR WHAT IS NOT.
cards: Before there was anything, a hymn in the Rig Veda says, there was neither what is nor what is not. No air, and no sky beyond it. No death, and no deathlessness, no sign of night or day.
Only the One, breathing without wind, by its own power. Darkness, hidden in darkness. Then, by the power of heat, the One came to be.

Desire came, the first seed of mind, and the sages, searching in their hearts, found the bond between what is and what is not. That's the creation story of the Nasadiya Sukta, chanted for around three thousand years.
And then it does something you might not expect from scripture.

teach.b: It asks. Who truly knows? Who here could say where this creation came from?
Even the gods, it says, came later than this making, so who knows where it arose? Then the last line. The one who watches over it all from the highest heaven surely knows.

teach.h: OR PERHAPS THAT ONE DOES NOT KNOW.
teach.b: Or perhaps that one does not know. Here's what that shows about this religion.
The Vedas are shruti, what was heard: Hinduism's oldest and most sacred texts, passed from teacher to student by memory, syllable by syllable, and still chanted that way.
And right inside them sits an honest question, kept as carefully as any prayer.
Hindu scripture holds more than one account of creation: a cosmic person in one hymn, a golden womb in another, and this one, which leaves the answer open.
Asking, in this tradition, is part of the path, not a threat to it.

Centuries later the Brahma Sutra would open with the words: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Next year the path climbs into the Vedas themselves: hymns to Agni, the fire, to Ushas, the dawn, and this one.

And today? When a child looks up at the stars and asks where it all came from, a Hindu parent can tell the old stories and also say: our oldest hymn asked that too, and left room for you to keep asking.
Faith here doesn't mean pretending to know.

how: Hymns of the Rig Veda are still chanted by memory in traditional recitation, passed from teacher to student, and the Nasadiya Sukta is often cited, by Hindus and others, as a sign that Hindu scripture makes room for open questions.

the Rig Veda hymn of creation that ends with a question
a hymn that names the god who made the world

s: Hindus must believe one fixed story of how the world began
the Rig Veda alone has several creation hymns, and this one ends in a question.
in the creation hymn, the gods came later than the making of the world
the hymn says so, and asks: then who knows where it arose?
the creation hymn ends with a firm answer
it ends: the one in the highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps does not know.

games.q: a classmate says religion is only about having answers, never asking questions. what in the Vedas would you point to?
o: the Nasadiya Sukta, a creation hymn that ends: or perhaps that one does not know.
nothing: the Vedas only give rules for rituals.
the hymn that names the maker and closes the case.
games.why: the Rig Veda's hymn of creation asks who truly knows, and ends in an open question. the tradition kept that question as scripture.

practice: Settle, and quietly ask the hymn's question: before all this, what was there? Don't reach for an answer; let the question stay in you, the way the sages searched in their hearts.

When the mind hurries to fill it, come back to the breath, which arrived before you asked for it. If you pray, rest before God, or the gods, with the question still open; if you don't, simply sit beside it.

wordCard.voice: Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation, the Rig Veda hymn that asks who really knows, and ends: or perhaps not.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the Nasadiya Sukta, named from its opening, 'then there was not non-being.' Rig Veda 10.129.
